enonce_markdown: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The half-life is a constant for each isotope and does not depend on the amount of the sample or on its conditions.

### Solution

After one half-life, half of the original parent atoms remain, after two half-lives a quarter, and so on. It is not the time for complete decay (decay never quite finishes), nor half the age of the rock, and the amount of daughter does not simply double in one half-life.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The time taken for the amount of daughter isotope to double
The time taken for half of the parent atoms in a sample to decay
Half of the time that has passed since the rock formed
The time taken for all of the parent atoms in a sample to decay

enonce_markdown: A piece of wood from an archaeological site is thought to be about 3000 years old. Which radiometric method is the most suitable for dating it?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A method works best when the age to be measured is of the same order as the half-life of the isotope used.

### Solution

In 3000 years about a third of the original carbon-14 will have decayed, which is easy to measure. The other isotopes have half-lives of billions of years, so in 3000 years almost no parent would have changed and the tiny amount of daughter could not be measured accurately.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Rubidium-87 to strontium-87 (half-life about 49 billion years)
Uranium-238 to lead-206 (half-life about 4.5 billion years)
Potassium-40 to argon-40 (half-life about 1.25 billion years)

enonce_markdown: A mineral grain contains an isotope with a half-life of 80 million years. Analysis shows that 12.5 % of the original parent atoms remain and that no daughter was present at the start. What is the age of the mineral?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Work out how many half-lives are needed to reduce the parent to the remaining fraction, then multiply by the half-life.

### Solution

$12.5\ \% = \tfrac{1}{8} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^3$, so three half-lives have passed: $3 \times 80 = 240$ million years. 160 million years would be two half-lives (25 % left), 400 million years would be five (3.1 % left), and 100 million years has no basis.

**Answer: A.**

enonce_markdown: The potassium-argon method is used to date a lava flow. What is the main assumption that makes the result meaningful?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Every radiometric clock assumes a known starting daughter content and a closed system since the clock was set.

### Solution

Argon is a gas that escapes from molten rock, so a freshly cooled lava has no radiogenic argon, and all the argon-40 found has come from the decay of potassium-40 since cooling, provided that none has leaked out or been added. Equal initial amounts, steady addition of atmospheric argon, or a half-life that varies with temperature would all make the age meaningless; the half-life is constant.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Argon-40 has been added steadily to the rock from the atmosphere since it formed
The half-life of potassium-40 changes with the temperature of the rock
Radiogenic argon-40 escaped from the molten lava, so the clock started when the rock cooled, and the minerals have stayed closed since
The lava contained equal amounts of potassium-40 and argon-40 when it cooled

enonce_markdown:
Zircon crystals from a granite have an atomic ratio of lead-206 to uranium-238 of 0.18, and all the lead-206 is the product of uranium decay. The half-life of uranium-238 is $4.47 \times 10^{9}$ years.

(a) Calculate the decay constant $\lambda$ of uranium-238 using $\lambda = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$.

(b) Use $t = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{P}\right)$ to calculate the age of the zircon.

(c) Why is zircon a good mineral for U-Pb dating?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The age follows from the ratio of daughter to parent atoms D/P and the decay constant: $t = \frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1 + D/P)$.

### Solution

(a) $\lambda = 0.6931 / (4.47 \times 10^{9}) = 1.55 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$.

(b) $t = \dfrac{1}{1.55 \times 10^{-10}} \ln(1.18) = 6.45 \times 10^{9} \times 0.1655 = 1.07 \times 10^{9}$ years, that is about 1070 million years (1.07 billion years).

(c) Zircon takes uranium into its crystal when it forms but rejects lead, so the lead present is the product of decay; it is also hard and chemically resistant, which keeps it a closed system through later heating and weathering, and it is common in granites.

enonce_markdown:
A granite from a mountain belt gives these ages: U-Pb on zircon, 600 million years; K-Ar on biotite mica, 540 million years. Assume closure temperatures of about 900 degrees Celsius for zircon (U-Pb) and about 300 degrees Celsius for biotite (K-Ar).

(a) Explain why the two ages are different although they come from the same rock.

(b) Which age is closest to the time of crystallisation of the granite, and what does the other age record?

(c) Calculate the average rate of cooling of the granite between the two closure temperatures, in degrees per million years.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A mineral starts to record time only when it has cooled below its closure temperature, the temperature below which parent and daughter atoms stop escaping.

### Solution

(a) Each mineral behaves as a closed system only below its own closure temperature. Zircon retains lead at very high temperature, so its clock started early when the granite magma crystallised. Biotite keeps argon only below about 300 degrees Celsius, so the argon clock started only after the granite had cooled to that temperature. Both ages are correct; they date different events.

(b) The **U-Pb zircon age (600 million years)** is closest to the age of crystallisation. The K-Ar biotite age (540 million years) is a **cooling age**: it records the time when the rock fell to about 300 degrees Celsius, for example during uplift and erosion.

(c) The granite cooled by $900 - 300 = 600$ degrees in $600 - 540 = 60$ million years, so the average rate is $600 / 60 = 10$ degrees per million years.
